chunks.title: Where to get help · FarmBot
chunks.heading: 1. KVK Koraput : ask about a pest, a disease or a sick patch, or ask for a field visit
chunks.text: What it is. Krishi Vigyan Kendra ( KVK ) Koraput is the farm science centre run by the Odisha agriculture university (OUAT) at Sunabeda. Its scientists advise farmers and visit fields: they report 75 visits to farmers' fields reaching 2,850 farmers. How to reach it. Phone +91-7008930482 , email kvk.koraput@ouat.ac.in , or go to the office: Post Box No-10, Sunabeda, Koraput 763002. Staff listed on the official page include Ms. Sunita Dandasena (Senior Scientist and Head), Mr. Binod Chandra Behera (Scientist, Agricultural Extension) and Mr. Sabek Kumar Hantal (Soil Science). When it helps.

chunks.title: Where to get help · FarmBot
chunks.heading: 1. KVK Koraput : ask about a pest, a disease or a sick patch, or ask for a field visit
chunks.text: Before any spraying, when FarmBot shows a pest or weak-patch warning, or when you see an insect or disease you don't know. Take a clear photo and a sample of the plant. Source: KVK Koraput contact page · KVK Koraput staff page · KVK Koraput : field visits (PDF)

chunks.title: Where to get help · FarmBot
chunks.heading: 2. Soil testing and the Soil Health Card
chunks.text: What it is. A lab test of your field's soil. The Soil Health Card shows the soil's nutrients and suggests how much fertiliser to use. The government pays for each sample (the Centre gives ₹190 per sample). KVK Koraput has its own soil lab and reports testing about 500 samples a year; it also handed out Soil Health Cards on 5 Dec 2024 . How to reach it. Ask KVK Koraput (phone above) or the Bandhugaon agriculture office whether there is any charge and how to send a sample. To take a sample: after harvest or when no crop is standing, dig a V-shaped cut 15–20 cm deep at the 4 corners and the centre of the field and mix the soil. When it helps.

chunks.title: Where to get help · FarmBot
chunks.heading: 2. Soil testing and the Soil Health Card
chunks.text: Right after the paddy harvest, before a winter crop or before buying fertiliser for next season. Source: PIB: Soil Health Card scheme · KVK Koraput : soil lab (PDF) · KVK Koraput : Soil Health Card day (PDF) · Koraput district: agriculture contacts

chunks.title: Where to get help · FarmBot
chunks.heading: 3. PMFBY crop insurance (Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana)
chunks.text: What it is. Government crop insurance for crop loss. For a winter crop, the last date to join is usually 31 Dec ; check the exact date with your bank or PACS. How to reach it. Join through your bank, the PACS (village cooperative), a Common Service Centre, or the PMFBY website . The name on the form must match your Aadhaar. Helpline 14447 (24×7). When it helps. Before the last date for each season. If an insured crop is damaged, report it within 72 hours on 14447. Source: PIB: PMFBY enrolment and helpline · PIB: report crop loss within 72 hours (PDF) · PMFBY website

chunks.title: Where to get help · FarmBot
chunks.heading: 4. Weather advice for farmers: GKMS bulletins and the Meghdoot app
chunks.text: What it is. The India Meteorological Department ( IMD ) publishes district farm-weather advice (Gramin Krishi Mausam Seva, GKMS) twice a week, on Tuesday and Friday. The Odisha bulletin was issued on 30 Oct 2026 . The free Meghdoot app shows the same advice on a phone. How to reach it. Install Meghdoot from the app store and choose Koraput , or read the Odisha bulletin and the IMD farm weather site . When it helps. Before spraying, irrigating or harvesting: it says when rain is due. Source: IMD Bhubaneswar farm weather bulletin (PDF) · Meghdoot app page · IMD agromet

chunks.title: Where to get help · FarmBot
chunks.heading: 5. riceXpert app (rice institute, Cuttack)
chunks.text: What it is. A free phone app from the National Rice Research Institute (ICAR- NRRI ), Cuttack, with advice on growing rice. How to reach it. Install it from Google Play . When it helps. To look up rice growing advice on the phone. Source: riceXpert on Google Play · NRRI : about riceXpert

chunks.title: Where to get help · FarmBot
chunks.heading: 6. Krushi Samrudhi helpline 155333 (Odisha)
chunks.text: What it is. The Odisha government's free farmer helpline. It also calls farmers with advice through the season. How to reach it. Call 155333 . The Krushak Odisha portal has the state farmer schemes. When it helps. For questions about Odisha farm schemes, or for advice by phone. Source: Krushi Samrudhi helpline · Krushak Odisha

chunks.title: Where to get help · FarmBot
chunks.heading: 7. Kisan Call Centre 1800 -180- 1551
chunks.text: What it is. The national free farmer phone line. In Odisha the calls are answered from Bhubaneswar, in Odia. How to reach it. Call 1800 -180- 1551 , 6 AM to 10 PM, all 7 days . When it helps. For a quick answer on a crop problem when KVK can't be reached. Source: Kisan Call Centre: about · PIB: Kisan Call Centres

chunks.title: Where to get help · FarmBot
chunks.heading: 8. KVK trainings and the growing guide
chunks.text: What it is. KVK Koraput runs short farmer trainings and publishes a growing guide (package of practices) that covers rice, black gram and mustard/toria. It has also tested a newer rice variety, OUAT Kalinga Rice-1, in Koraput . How to reach it. Ask KVK Koraput (phone above) for the next training dates, or open the guide below. When it helps. Before choosing a winter crop or a new rice variety. Source: KVK Koraput : growing guide (PDF) · KVK Koraput : training calendar, Dec 2025 (PDF) · KVK Koraput : Kalinga Rice-1 test (PDF)

chunks.text: A short guide for anyone new to this. No background needed. FarmBot is a farm helper for the paddy fields of Nilabadi ; it follows a few plots closely today, and more fields will be added over time. The short version

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: What the satellite sees
chunks.text: A photo about every 5 days . Free European photo satellites pass over Nilabadi and take a photo of the area about every 5 days . FarmBot downloads these photos for free. Each photo is made of 10 m squares. One square is about the size of a small house plot. The satellite can't see single plants, only the average colour of each square. Greenness means a healthy, leafy crop. Healthy leaves reflect a lot of invisible light that cameras on the satellite can measure. From that, FarmBot works out a greenness score from 0 to 1. A bare field scores low. A thick green paddy crop scores high. Watching greenness week by week shows the crop's life.

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: What the satellite sees
chunks.text: The score rises when the crop starts growing (green-up), is highest when it is fully grown (peak), and falls as it ripens and is harvested. These are the crop life stages . It also sees open water. A water score shows how much of the Panchayat Pond has open water on its surface. Be careful

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: What it can't see
chunks.text: Through clouds. In the monsoon the sky is often cloudy. Cloudy parts of a photo are thrown away ( cloud removal ). In July and August 2026 there were only one or two clear photos, so there are gaps just when the crop is planted. A radar satellite that sees through clouds now fills in rough planting dates. Pests and diseases, directly. Insects are far too small, and early disease doesn't change the colour of a 10 m square. Pest levels come from the weather (heat, rain and humidity that pests like), and are not yet tested here. Later, sensors, insect traps and cameras on the fields will add ground checks. See Pest alerts . How much grain you'll get.

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: What it can't see
chunks.text: Greenness only lets FarmBot compare this year with last year. It can't give a harvest weight in tonnes. Soil and rain on your own field. Soil and weather numbers on this site are computer estimates for a wider area. There is no rain gauge or soil test on the farm yet. Exact field edges. The outlines were traced by hand, not surveyed. Areas are approximate. FarmBot is an experiment. It uses satellites only for now. Always trust what you see in the field first. What the numbers mean

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: The numbers on this site, in plain words
chunks.text: Number What it means Example from this site Greenness score (0 to 1) How green and leafy the crop looks. Under 0.4 : dry or empty field. 0.4 – 0.65 : young crop. 0.65 or more: fully green crop. Temple plot on 23 Oct : 0.87 , a fully green crop. Water score Whether a square is open water. Above 0 means water. The Panchayat Pond had 0.25 ha of open water on 23 Oct , at most 0.40 ha . Yield comparison score This year's greenness against last year's, over the same dates. 1.00 = the same as last year. It is not tonnes of grain. Fishing Pond plot 0.89 : a little behind last year, mostly because it was planted later. Temple plot 1.10 : greener.

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: The numbers on this site, in plain words
chunks.text: Millimetres (mm) of rain How deep the rain would stand on flat ground. June–October 2026 : about 1,402 mm . 6 months had under 25 mm . Water pulled out by sun and wind How much water heat and wind take out of wet ground, in mm. More than the rain means the field is drying out. About 1,599 mm a year here. Hectare (ha) A unit of land, 100 m by 100 m . 1 ha is about 2.47 acres . Temple plot: 7.47 ha ( 18.5 acres ). Fishing Pond plot: 2.49 ha ( 6.2 acres ). 10 m square The smallest dot in a satellite photo. The Fishing Pond plot holds about 250 of them, so detail inside a plot is rough.

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: The numbers on this site, in plain words
chunks.text: The words Seen by satellite , Estimate and Experimental appear next to numbers across the site, so you know where each one comes from. Word list

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Every term on the site, explained
chunks.text: In alphabetical order. The technical name is shown small, in case you see it elsewhere. 10 m square The smallest square in a satellite photo, 10 m by 10 m ( 100 square metres). A field of 1 hectare holds about 100 of them. Squares on a field edge often mix in bunds or the next field. Technical name: Pixel Cloud removal Each photo comes with a map of which squares are cloud, cloud shadow or haze. Those squares are thrown away. A date counts only if most of the field is clear.

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Every term on the site, explained
chunks.text: Technical name: Cloud mask Crop life stages The crop's stages as seen from space: green-up (the crop starts growing and the field turns green), peak (the greenest point), and ripening (leaves turn yellow, so greenness falls before harvest). Technical name: Phenology Estimate Worked out by a computer weather or soil model for a big area, not measured on these fields. Good for trends, not for exact amounts. Technical name: Modelled Experimental A first try. It may change once ground checks or more seasons are available. Technical name: Experimental Greenness score How green and leafy the crop looks from space, on a scale from 0 to 1.

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Every term on the site, explained
chunks.text: Healthy, thick leaves reflect a lot of invisible near-infrared light, and the score uses that. On this site, under 0.4 means a dry or empty field, 0.4 to 0.65 a young crop, and 0.65 or more a fully green crop. Technical name: NDVI (Normalised Difference Vegetation Index) Half-way green date The rough date when the field got half-way from its dry-season low to its green peak. Technical name: Green-up ( 50% point) Haze-corrected photos The version of the photos that has been cleaned of haze in the air, so colours are closer to what the ground really looks like. Technical name: Level-2A (L2A) Hectare A unit of land area: 100 m by 100 m , or 10,000 square metres. 1 hectare is about 2.47 acres .

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Every term on the site, explained
chunks.text: Technical name: ha Humidity How much moisture is in the air, in per cent. 100% is fully saturated, like fog or dew. Technical name: RH (relative humidity) Land-use map A free 2021 map by the European Space Agency that labels every 10 m square as crop fields, trees, grass, buildings or water. FarmBot uses it to leave out trees, buildings and water near the plots. Technical name: ESA WorldCover 2021 Lining up a screenshot Fitting a phone map screenshot onto real map positions by matching roads, ponds and tree clumps. Technical name: Georeferencing Metre map grid The map grid FarmBot 's map files use. It measures position in metres, so areas and distances come out right.

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Every term on the site, explained
chunks.text: Readers of this site don't need it. Technical name: UTM zone 44N ( EPSG:32644 ) Millimetres of rain How deep the water would be on flat ground if none soaked in or ran off. 25 mm in a month is very little. A heavy monsoon month here can bring several hundred. Technical name: mm Monsoon crop season The main rain-fed paddy season, roughly June to November. Technical name: Kharif NASA weather estimates Free daily weather estimates from NASA , the United States space agency, on a grid about 50 km wide. Technical name: NASA POWER Online photo catalogue The free online library from which FarmBot downloads the satellite photos. It lists every photo by date and place.

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Every term on the site, explained
chunks.text: Technical name: STAC catalogue, Microsoft Planetary Computer Open-Meteo A free weather service. FarmBot uses its rebuilt past weather for rain, soil wetness and water pulled out by sun and wind. Technical name: Open-Meteo historical weather Pheromone trap A small trap that uses a scent to attract the male moths of one pest. Counting the catch shows when that pest is active. Technical name: Pheromone trap Photo satellite A pair of free European satellites that photograph the area about every 5 days . They take photos in visible and invisible light. Each photo is made of 10 m by 10 m squares. Technical name: Sentinel-2 Radar echo How much of the radar signal bounces back.

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Every term on the site, explained
chunks.text: Still water reflects it away, so a flooded field looks dark. It gets brighter as the crop grows. Technical name: Backscatter Radar satellite A free European radar satellite. Radar sends its own signal and sees through clouds, so it works in the monsoon. It shows standing water well. FarmBot uses it to find when fields were flooded for planting. Technical name: Sentinel-1 Ripening The stage when paddy leaves dry and turn yellow-brown as the grain fills. The greenness score falls steadily. Technical name: Senescence Seen by satellite Read directly from satellite photos of these fields. Technical name: Satellite-observed Smoothed line Single photos jump up and down because of haze and light.

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Every term on the site, explained
chunks.text: The smoothed line takes the middle value of all photos within 10 days either side of each date, so the trend is easier to see. Technical name: 20-day running median Soil wetness How much of the soil is water. It is shown for the top 7 cm and for 28 to 100 cm deep. These are computer estimates, not measured on the farm. Technical name: Soil moisture Spread band The shaded band around a line shows where the middle half of the field's squares fell on each date. Technical name: 25th to 75th percentile Water pulled out by sun and wind How much water the sun, heat and wind pull out of wet soil and plants each day, in millimetres. If this is more than the rain, the field is drying out.

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Every term on the site, explained
chunks.text: Technical name: ET0 (reference evapotranspiration) Water score How much open water or wetness shows in a spot. Above 0 means open water. There are two versions. They use slightly different colours of light and give slightly different pond sizes. Technical name: NDWI and MNDWI (water indexes) Weak patch A part of a field that stays less green than the rest, year after year. It could mean poor soil, waterlogging or pests, and is a place to go and look. Technical name: Weak zone Weather rebuilt by computer Past weather worked out by a computer from many weather stations and satellites, on a grid about 9 to 11 km wide.

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Every term on the site, explained
chunks.text: Technical name: Reanalysis Who's who in the sources ICAR is the Indian Council of Agricultural Research, the government's farm research body. NRRI is the National Rice Research Institute in Cuttack (its old name was CRRI ). NCIPM is ICAR 's National Centre for Integrated Pest Management. NICRA is ICAR 's national project on climate-resilient farming. IIRR is the Indian Institute of Rice Research. IRRI is the International Rice Research Institute. IMD is the India Meteorological Department, the weather office. IPM means integrated pest management: scouting, traps, and spraying only when needed. LGD is the government's Local Government Directory of villages.

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Every term on the site, explained
chunks.text: Technical name: ICAR , NRRI ( CRRI ), NCIPM , NICRA , IIRR , IRRI , IMD , IPM, LGD Winter crop season The dry winter season after the paddy harvest. Crops such as green gram, black gram or mustard can be grown then if there is water. Technical name: Rabi World soil map A free world soil map from ISRIC (the International Soil Reference and Information Centre). It estimates soil type on a 250 m grid. It is a prediction, not a test of this soil. Technical name: ISRIC SoilGrids 2.0 Year-to-year match score A number from -1 to 1 that says whether the same squares were low in both years. Near 1 means the same squares were low both times. Near 0, or below 0, means no pattern.

chunks.title: What the satellite sees, and what it can't · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Every term on the site, explained
chunks.text: Technical name: Spearman rank correlation Yield comparison score A score comparing how green this year's crop was against last year's, over the same dates. It is not a harvest weight in tonnes. 1.00 means the same as last year. Above 1 means greener. Below 1 means less green. Technical name: Relative yield index Want the formulas? See Sources and method .

chunks.title: FarmBot · Nilabadi farm helper
chunks.heading: Three jobs, in order
chunks.text: FarmBot is a farming helper for the paddy fields of Nilabadi . Today it follows two plots closely, using free satellite photos and computer weather estimates. Next paddy season it will add sensors, insect traps and cameras on the fields. Job 1 · working draft, untested Pest and disease weather check Each week: does the weather suit stem borer, gall midge, leaf folder, brown planthopper, blast, sheath blight or bacterial leaf blight? This week: Blast high at the Fishing Pond plot (its field-level alerts are on its plot page), with photos to spot each pest. The rules are not yet checked against pest counts here, so ask KVK Koraput before spraying.

chunks.title: FarmBot · Nilabadi farm helper
chunks.heading: Three jobs, in order
chunks.text: → Job 2 · working draft Weekly advice A short note each week for each plot, on its plot page: the crop's stage, pest weather, heavy rain days and dry spells, and links to the newest official farm advice for Koraput . → Job 3 · experimental Is this year's crop better or worse? A yield comparison score compares how green the crop is with last season. It is a comparison, not tonnes of grain. The Fishing Pond plot looks a little behind last year, mostly because it was planted later. A fair comparison is possible only after harvest. The Temple plot is greener than last year. → More checks · first versions When will it be ready to harvest? Not ripening yet.

chunks.title: FarmBot · Nilabadi farm helper
chunks.heading: Three jobs, in order
chunks.text: Rough window: about 15 Nov – 5 Dec 2026 (estimate), Temple plot likely first. Weak patches in a plot A possible weak patch in the south-west part of the Fishing Pond plot (about 0.2 ha ). None in the Temple plot. Worth a walk. Radar that sees through cloud Radar shows the Fishing Pond plot was planted mid-to-late August 2026 and the Temple plot around mid-August (± 12 days ). Winter crop water (estimate) Water already comes from the small Panchayat Pond across the road. At an assumed depth of about 1.5 m (not measured), it could stretch to roughly 0.6–0.7 ha of green gram or black gram after the harvest. The real depth still needs measuring.

chunks.text: They were drawn from the maps you marked and lined up with close-up aerial photos (to within about 1–2 m ). The edges are right to about 5–10 m . The photos are coarse. Each 10 m square is one dot of colour. The Fishing Pond plot holds only about 250 of these squares, and the ones on its edge mix in bunds and the next field. chunks.text: FarmBot watches each plot's greenness fall as the grain ripens and the field turns golden ( ripening ). Every photo since 23 Oct has been cloudy, so there is no newer reading. Rough harvest window: about 15 Nov – 5 Dec 2026 (an estimate, not a forecast). Last year both plots went from green to bare between about 10 and 22 Nov 2025 . chunks.heading: Radar that sees through clouds Seen by satellite
chunks.text: A radar satellite passes about every 12 days and sees through monsoon cloud. Standing water on a paddy field makes the radar echo dark; it gets brighter again as the rice grows. So the darkest pass in the monsoon shows roughly when the field was flooded for transplanting. Dates are good to about ± 12 days , one pass either way. How to read this: a deep dip in the monsoon is the field flooded for planting. The rise after it is the crop growing. Radar echo inside each plot, 53 passes from 6 Jan 2025 to 23 Oct 2026 .

chunks.heading: How far could the Panchayat Pond stretch to a winter crop? Experimental
chunks.text: After the paddy harvest, a short winter crop such as green gram (moong), black gram (biri) or mustard could follow on the Fishing Pond plot. The only water source counted here is the Panchayat Pond : the small road-side pond just across the road, north of the plot. It belongs to the local Panchayat, and water is already drawn from it for the plot. The village fishing pond's water can't be used, so it is not counted. This works out how far that same pond could stretch to a winter crop .

chunks.title: Advice, yield and harvest · FarmBot
chunks.heading: How far could the Panchayat Pond stretch to a winter crop? Experimental
chunks.text: It counts the water each crop uses (from drying by sun and wind and the crop's stage), the little winter rain that helps, water lost on the way to the plants, the water the pond itself loses to the sun, and a share kept back for the water already being drawn. Sowing is taken as 1 December, after the harvest. What to know first The depth is assumed, not measured: 1.5 m , about as deep as a typical swimming pool. Nobody has measured the pond yet. The table below also shows 1.0 m and 2.0 m . A marked pole would settle it. Water already used: assumed to take about 25% of what the pond holds after its own drying. This is a guess; the real share is not known.

chunks.heading: How far could the Panchayat Pond stretch to a winter crop? Experimental
chunks.text: The big number is a normal winter; in brackets a dry winter (only 1 winter in 5 is drier). Every depth is assumed, not measured. 25% of the water is set aside for the use already made of the pond (assumed). 1 mm over 1 ha is 10 cubic metres of water. What this says At the assumed 1.5 m , the pond could water about 0.63–0.70 ha of black gram or green gram from today's open water. That is roughly a quarter of the 2.49 ha plot. Longer mustard needs much more water: about 0.32 ha . If the pond is only 1.0 m deep, that falls to about 0.38–0.43 ha , because the pond loses about 22–24 cm to the sun over the winter whatever you do. Clearing some weeds helps.

chunks.title: Advice, yield and harvest · FarmBot
chunks.heading: How far could the Panchayat Pond stretch to a winter crop? Experimental
chunks.text: At its fullest open water, 1.5 m would water about 1.13 ha of green gram. Water under the weeds is not seen by the satellite, so the real amount is not known. The open water shrinks in winter. Last December it was only about 0.10 ha , less than half of today's. Winter rain hardly helps. Over December–February the middle winter had about 41 mm of rain ( Open-Meteo ) or 17 mm ( NASA ), over 25 winters, and most of it is too light to reach the roots. Why the real numbers may differ The depth and the water already used are assumptions. A measured depth and a rough count of pumping hours would replace them.

chunks.heading: How far could the Panchayat Pond stretch to a winter crop? Experimental
chunks.text: Leftover soil wetness after paddy is not counted , so the land that can be watered is probably more . The rice institute says it can supply 55–80% of a winter crop's water in rice fallows. Water seeping out of the pond bottom is not known . It lowers the numbers. The crop water needs come from world crop tables, not from Koraput trials. Black gram uses the green gram values. Half of the pumped water is assumed lost on the way and in the field (open channels and flooding small basins). If the Fishing Pond plot is harvested in early December, sowing could slip to mid-December.

chunks.text: Mustard is best sown in September–October, but late sowing from mid-November to mid-December is common in eastern India after a late paddy harvest (Rice Knowledge Bank, Odisha). Sources and method (for specialists) Crop water use = crop factor × reference drying (FAO-56 single crop coefficient), stages 20/30/30/ 20% of the season. Useful rain per 30 days by the FAO method. Pond loss = 1.05 × reference drying minus rain. Hectares = open water × (assumed depth − pond loss) × (1 − 0.25 already used) ÷ water to pump per hectare. Open water = water score above 0 inside the traced pond outline on cloud-free Sentinel-2 photos ( 102 photos , 1 Oct 2025 to 23 Oct 2026 ).

chunks.text: A plot compared only with itself can't tell a bad season from a weak field. So FarmBot found paddy fields within about 2 km of each plot from space and gave each the same yield comparison score : greenness on 1–23 October this year divided by last year. If every field dropped, the season was poor; if only the followed plot dropped, look at that plot. Fields are described only by direction and distance. No owners. The short answer Fishing Pond plot: about the same as its neighbours. Its score ( 0.94 ) sits right in the middle of the neighbouring paddy ( 0.94 ). Most paddy around it is also a little less green than last October, so a good part of its drop is the season, not the field.

chunks.title: Sources and method · FarmBot
chunks.heading: How the numbers are made
chunks.text: The plots. Outlines were traced from the map screenshots on which you marked the fields. The Fishing Pond plot ( 2.49 ha ( 6.2 acres )) was redrawn as one outline from your close-up screenshot on 31 Oct 2026 . The Temple plot is one block north of the road, opposite the Agnigangamma Temple ( 7.47 ha ( 18.5 acres )). The Panchayat Pond north of the Fishing Pond plot was traced from the close-up aerial photo ( 0.81 ha ( 2.00 acres )). Each screenshot was lined up with close-up aerial photos by matching roads, ponds and tree clumps, to within about 1 m . The Fishing Pond outline follows the bunds you can see. The temple outline follows the hand-drawn ring, kept 4 m back from the road.

chunks.title: Sources and method · FarmBot
chunks.heading: How the numbers are made
chunks.text: They are not surveyed boundaries. Crop greenness. FarmBot uses every cloud-free satellite photo from 1 Oct 2025 to 23 Oct 2026 . For each one it takes the middle greenness score of the 10 m squares whose centre is inside each outline. Squares that the land-use map labels trees, buildings or water are dropped. A photo only counts when at least 60% of those squares are clear of cloud. The values are then smoothed . From the smoothed line FarmBot reads the greenest point, the dates it fell below 0.7 and 0.5 , the dry-season low, and the half-way green date. Pond water.

chunks.title: Sources and method · FarmBot
chunks.heading: How the numbers are made
chunks.text: Squares inside the traced Panchayat Pond outline (plus 10 m ) where the water score is above 0 count as open water, and are added up in hectares, on photos where at least 80% of that area is clear of cloud. Water under floating weeds is not counted. Locations. The pond was found by matching a map screenshot to water seen by the satellite. The temple position comes from a public map listing (plus code X768+5R7 ), checked against photos and OpenStreetMap . The lined-up screenshot puts its pin within about 6 m of that point. Weekly update. A script builds the site from the data folders. It can be re-run each week after new photos are downloaded.

chunks.title: Sources and method · FarmBot
chunks.heading: How the numbers are made
chunks.text: How to read this: the lines are roads and the river from the free OpenStreetMap . They line up with the photo, which shows the location is right. OpenStreetMap roads and river over a satellite photo ( 21 Oct 2026 ) around the temple, used to check the location. © OpenStreetMap contributors. Advice and checks ( experimental ). Yield comparison: the middle greenness of each plot on cloud-free photos (at least 60% clear) in the same 1–23 October window, 2025 against 2026. Harvest heads-up: the weekly change in the smoothed greenness. Weak patches: each square's greenness minus the field's middle value, taken over each October's cloud-free photos.

chunks.title: Sources and method · FarmBot
chunks.heading: How the numbers are made
chunks.text: Only squares fully inside the outline are tested. Both plots leave out a 10 m strip round the edge. A square counts as weak if it is in the lowest 20% in both seasons. Winter water: each crop's water use from the drying by sun and wind and its stage (world crop tables), minus the part of the winter rain that reaches the roots, divided by 50% to cover losses on the way; compared with the pond's latest open-water area for each metre of usable depth, after the pond's own drying. 25 winters of Open-Meteo weather. Neighbours: paddy within 2 km found by the dry-season, radar-flooding and October tests, grouped into 50 m patches, each given the same October score. Radar.

chunks.title: Sources and method · FarmBot
chunks.heading: How the numbers are made
chunks.text: Radar satellite passes about every 12 days ( 53 passes , 6 Jan 2025 to 23 Oct 2026 ). The darkest monsoon pass inside each outline is taken as the flooding for transplanting, so dates are good to about ± 12 days . The road-side strip of the Fishing Pond plot (within 50 m of the Panchayat Pond) is compared with the rest of the plot on every pass. Pest weather check ( experimental , untested). The rules are copied unchanged from the government and rice-research documents listed below ( who's who ). Each week's weather (recent weather plus the Open-Meteo forecast) is checked against them, only at the crop stages when each pest does damage.

chunks.title: Sources and method · FarmBot
chunks.heading: How the numbers are made
chunks.text: They have not been checked against pest counts in Koraput . Weekly advice. Brings together the crop stage, the pest check, heavy rain days ( 40 mm or more) and dry spells from the forecast, and the newest official advice from KVK Koraput , IMD and NRRI . Links are checked before each build. No pesticide doses. Harvest heads-up. Each week new photos are checked for cloud. The latest clear greenness is compared with the same week last year, and last year's drop dates are shifted by the radar planting dates to give a rough window. Technical details (for specialists) Photos: Sentinel-2 Level-2A (haze-corrected), from the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC catalogue, tiles 44QQF/44QQG.

chunks.title: Sources and method · FarmBot
chunks.heading: How the numbers are made
chunks.text: Map grid: UTM zone 44N ( EPSG:32644 ). Bands are colours of light: B03 green, B04 red, B08 near-infrared (invisible), B11 short-wave infrared (invisible). NDVI = (B08−B04)/(B08+B04). NDWI = (B03−B08)/(B03+B08). MNDWI = (B03−B11)/(B03+B11). Clear squares for NDVI are the scene classes vegetation, bare soil and water. A − 1000 offset is applied for processing baseline 4 and later. Crop series: median NDVI inside the outline, 20-day running median, peak, 0.7 and 0.5 crossings, dry-season floor and 50% amplitude green-up. Only WorldCover class 40 (cropland). Lining up screenshots: SIFT keypoint matching with a rotation-scale-shift fit and outlier rejection, against Esri World Imagery.

chunks.title: Sources and method · FarmBot
chunks.heading: How the numbers are made
chunks.text: Weak zones: Spearman rank correlation of per-pixel anomalies between Octobers 2025 and 2026 ; bottom- 20% cut in both seasons. Radar: Sentinel-1 RTC (radiometrically terrain corrected) from the Planetary Computer , one descending orbit, median VV and VH backscatter in dB per outline; dip = lowest VV+VH sum between 1 Jun and 30 Sep . Pest check: standard meteorological weeks; insect rules use the previous week's weather; leaf wetness estimated from rain and RH ≥ 90% . Open-Meteo forecast for the coming 16 days .

chunks.title: Nilabadi pest alerts · FarmBot
chunks.heading: What to look for in the field
chunks.text: The alerts only become trustworthy for Koraput once they are compared with what is actually seen in the fields. A simple weekly note (date, field, count) is enough. One season of notes would let us test the rules. What to check How When the number matters Source Stem borer and leaf folder moths A light trap (a bulb over a pan of water) by the field, or 4-5 pheromone traps per acre (lure traps sold for "yellow stem borer" and "leaf folder"). Count the moths each morning and add them up for the week. 4-5 male moths in one pheromone trap ( NRRI ). In the rule tables, 1 moth per square metre or 25 moths per trap per week.

chunks.text: NRRI advisory Oct 2026 ; NCIPM bulletin Annexure II Dead hearts and white ears (stem borer) Walk a diagonal across the field and look at 20 hills. Count dried central shoots (dead hearts) before flowering, and white empty ears after flowering. 10% dead hearts at tillering; 2% white ears NCIPM Annexure II Folded leaves (leaf folder) On the same 20 hills, count leaves rolled lengthwise with a caterpillar inside. 2 damaged leaves per hill NCIPM Annexure II; NRRI Silver shoots (gall midge) Before the ear forms, look for onion-leaf-like hollow tubes in place of a leaf.

chunks.title: Spot the pest · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Yellow stem borer
chunks.text: A small moth. Its caterpillars bore into the rice stem and eat it from the inside. Yellow stem borer moth resting on a rice stem. Photo: Md.Farhan Nabil · CC BY-SA 4.0 · source · resized A damaged stem split open to show where a stem borer fed inside (the label means "borer"). This one is the striped stem borer, a close relative; all rice stem borers cause deadhearts and whiteheads. Photo: Miquel Pujol Palol · CC BY-SA 3.0 · source · resized What to look for Young crop: a dried, brown centre shoot. It pulls out easily from the base. This is called a deadheart . After the ears come out: a white, empty ear that stands straight up, with no grain inside. This is called a whitehead .

chunks.title: Spot the pest · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Yellow stem borer
chunks.text: Tiny holes on the stem, and droppings inside the stem when you split it open. Where on the plant: Inside the stem. The moths rest on the leaves. When in the season: Any stage. Deadhearts while the crop is still putting out new shoots; whiteheads from ear forming to ripening. Easy to mix up with: Rat damage, neck blast and black bug can also leave dead shoots or white ears. To be sure, pull a damaged stem and split it: a stem borer caterpillar or its droppings will be inside. Source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank: stem borer . This week's alert level → Insect · 2 of 7

chunks.title: Spot the pest · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Gall midge
chunks.text: A tiny fly. Its maggot feeds inside the growing tip of a shoot. Photo coming No openly licensed photo of this one was found yet, so this entry is words only. FarmBot does not use made-up or computer-drawn pest pictures. What to look for A shoot that has turned into a hollow, silvery-white tube , about 1 cm wide and 10–30 cm long, instead of a leaf. It looks like an onion leaf, so it is called onion leaf or silver shoot . That shoot never makes an ear. Stunted plants with twisted or rolled leaves. Where on the plant: At the base of the shoot, where new shoots grow. When in the season: While the crop is still putting out new shoots. Cloudy, rainy weather suits it.

chunks.title: Spot the pest · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Gall midge
chunks.text: Easy to mix up with: Drought, potash shortage, salty soil, some virus diseases and thrips can also stunt plants or roll the leaves. Only gall midge makes the hollow silver tube; split it to find the small maggot. Source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank: rice gall midge . This week's alert level → Insect · 3 of 7

chunks.title: Spot the pest · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Leaf folder
chunks.text: A small moth. Its caterpillar folds a leaf around itself with silk and eats inside the fold. A rice leaf folded into a tube, with the leaf folder caterpillar inside. Photo: Badal Chandra Sarker · CC BY-SA 4.0 · source · resized The leaf folder moth: small, yellowish-brown with dark wavy bands on the wings. Photo: Haneesh K M. · CC0 · source · resized What to look for Leaves folded lengthwise into a tube , with a green caterpillar inside. Long, white, see-through streaks on the leaf where the green part was eaten. In bad cases, the field looks scorched, with many folded leaves. Where on the plant: On the leaves, most of all the youngest leaves and the top leaf (flag leaf).

chunks.title: Spot the pest · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Leaf folder
chunks.text: When in the season: From when new shoots grow to flowering. Damage to the flag leaf at ear time matters most. More common in shady, heavily fertilised parts of the field. Easy to mix up with: Gall midge and thrips can also roll leaves. Open the fold: a leaf folder fold has a caterpillar and silk inside. Source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank: rice leaffolder . This week's alert level → Insect · 4 of 7

chunks.title: Spot the pest · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Brown planthopper (BPH)
chunks.text: A tiny brown insect, about the size of a rice grain, that sucks sap at the base of the plants. A brown planthopper on a rice stem, photographed in India. Photo: portioid · CC BY 4.0 · source · resized Hopperburn: a dried, brown patch in a rice field caused by planthoppers (Japan). Photo: つくる暮らし · CC BY 2.0 · source · resized What to look for Small brown insects at the base of the plants , just above the water. Bend a plant slightly and tap it near the base: they fall onto the water. Round patches where plants turn orange-yellow, then brown and dry, as if burnt. This is called hopperburn . Black sooty mould at the base of the plants.

chunks.title: Spot the pest · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Brown planthopper (BPH)
chunks.text: Where on the plant: At the base of the stems, near the water. Not on the leaf tops. When in the season: From the growing stage to the milk stage of the grain. Checking after the milk stage is not needed. Easy to mix up with: Rice black bug can also dry plants in patches ("bugburn"). Look for the brown insects and the sooty mould at the base to be sure it is planthopper. Source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank: planthopper . This week's alert level → Disease · 5 of 7

chunks.title: Spot the pest · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Blast (leaf and neck)
chunks.text: A fungus disease. It can hit the leaves, the joints of the stem, and the neck just below the ear. A typical eye-shaped blast spot on a rice leaf: grey centre, brown edge. Photo: Yulin Jia, USDA Agricultural Research Service · public domain (US government work) · source · resized Ears hit by neck blast: the neck below the ear has turned grey-brown and the grains stay empty (label in Catalan). Photo: Miquel Pujol Palol · CC BY-SA 3.0 · source · resized What to look for On leaves: eye-shaped or diamond-shaped spots, pointed at both ends, with a grey or whitish centre and a reddish-brown edge. New spots are small, grey-green with a dark green edge. Spots can join and kill the whole leaf.

chunks.title: Spot the pest · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Blast (leaf and neck)
chunks.text: Neck blast: the neck just below the ear turns grey-brown and rots; the ear bends or breaks and stays empty or half-filled. Where on the plant: Leaf spots on the leaves; neck blast at the top of the stem, just below the ear. When in the season: Any stage. Leaf blast is worst on young crops; neck blast shows at flowering and grain filling. Long hours of wet leaves and cool nights suit it. Easy to mix up with: Brown spot is the main look-alike: its spots are rounder, brown, and have a yellow ring around them. Blast spots are longer, pointed and grey in the middle. Source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank: blast (leaf and collar) · ICAR- NRRI Technology Bulletin 277: rice blast .

chunks.title: Spot the pest · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Sheath blight
chunks.text: A fungus disease that starts low on the plant, near the water, and climbs up. Sheath blight on a rice leaf: pale grey-white patches with wavy brown edges. Photo: Peggy Greb, USDA Agricultural Research Service · public domain (US government work) · source · resized What to look for Oval, grey-green patches , about 1–3 cm long, on the leaf sheath (the part that wraps the stem), just above the water line. The patches grow and climb to the upper sheaths and the leaves. Older patches have a grey-white centre and a brown edge , often in a wavy, map-like pattern. Small, hard brown lumps (the fungus's resting bodies) on or near the patches.

chunks.title: Spot the pest · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Sheath blight
chunks.text: Where on the plant: Low on the stem, near the water line first, then higher up. When in the season: From when new shoots grow to the milk stage. Hot, very humid weather, a thick crop and a lot of nitrogen fertiliser suit it. Easy to mix up with: Stem rot and stem borer damage can look alike low on the stem. Sheath blight has the grey-white patches with brown, wavy edges, and the small brown lumps. Source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank: sheath blight · ICAR- NRRI Technology Bulletin 279: sheath blight . This week's alert level → Disease · 7 of 7

chunks.title: Spot the pest · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Bacterial leaf blight (BLB)
chunks.text: A disease caused by bacteria. It spreads fast after storms and heavy rain. Bacterial leaf blight: pale yellow-straw stripes with wavy edges running down from the leaf tips. Photo: Donald Groth, Louisiana State University AgCenter, Bugwood.org · CC BY 3.0 us · source · resized What to look for Yellow to straw-coloured stripes starting at the leaf tip or edge and running down the leaf, with a wavy edge . Early in the morning, small milky drops on young stripes; later they dry into tiny yellow beads. In young plants, leaves turn grey-green, roll up and the whole seedling wilts and dies (called kresek ). Where on the plant: On the leaf blades, from the tip and edges downwards.

chunks.title: Spot the pest · FarmBot
chunks.heading: Bacterial leaf blight (BLB)
chunks.text: When in the season: Any stage, worst when it starts early. Strong wind, heavy rain and a lot of nitrogen fertiliser favour it. Easy to mix up with: Kresek can look like stem borer damage, but a kresek plant does not pull out easily. Quick test: cut a young stripe, stand it in a clear glass of water and hold it to the light. A cloudy stream from the cut end means bacteria. Source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank: bacterial blight · ICAR- NRRI Technology Bulletin 276: bacterial leaf blight . This week's alert level → Not sure? Take a photo to the KVK .

They can confirm the pest or disease and say what to do. All official contacts → FarmBot gives no spray doses. Ask KVK Koraput or the agriculture officer before spraying.

How to read this: the blue line is wetness in the top 7 cm of soil, the orange line at 28–100 cm deep. The grey line is how much water the sun and wind pull out each day. When grey is high and blue falls, the soil is drying. Soil wetness and water pulled out by sun and wind (computer estimates). Technical name: soil moisture and ET0 Water · seen by satellite

chunks.text: The small Panchayat Pond across the road from the Fishing Pond plot is the water source already used for that plot. Its open water was 0.25 ha on 23 Oct , at most 0.40 ha between 1 Oct 2025 and 23 Oct 2026 , out of a 0.81 ha outline mostly under weeds (by the water score ). The satellite can't see depth. Seen by satellite 6 months had under 25 mm of rain. So the water left in the pond in the dry months is what matters for any winter crop ( winter crop water ). The village fishing pond's water can't be used, so it is not tracked. How to read this: higher means more open water. Water under weeds is not counted.
